vignette:
He is nineteen, a young African man who works as a UX designer for a small startup, and when he first talks about what happened, he does it in the same careful, structured way he describes a product flow. He starts at the beginning, trying to make it make sense.

The stalking begins near the end of his first year of working full-time. Because he is young and talented, he spends long hours online, sharing design drafts, joining feedback groups, and posting snippets of his work. At first, the messages from one follower seem flattering. The person praises his designs, comments within minutes of every post, and sends long notes saying no one understands his creativity the way they do. He tells himself it is strange but harmless. He does not want to seem dramatic.

Then the messages become constant. If he does not reply, the follower sends more: asking where he is, why he is ignoring them, whether he is with someone else. They begin referencing details he never remembers sharing-his neighborhood café, the color of the hoodie he wore in a story, the days he works late. He feels the first real jolt of fear one evening when he leaves the office and sees someone across the street lift a phone toward him, then turn away. He walks home telling himself it could be anyone, but he checks behind him three times before reaching his building.

After that, his world grows narrow. The messages turn angry, then pleading, then threatening. The stalker creates new accounts after he blocks them. They send screenshots of his online activity and photos taken from a distance: him at his desk near the office window, him waiting for coffee, him getting off a bus. He stops posting his work publicly, then stops going out unless he has to. At night he pushes a chair under his apartment door even though he knows it would not really stop anyone. He sleeps lightly, waking at every sound in the hallway, his heart already racing before he is fully conscious.

One afternoon at work, while presenting a prototype to his team, his phone lights up with a message from an unknown number: I can see you today. His mouth goes dry. He loses his place mid-sentence and stares at the screen too long. A coworker asks if he is okay, and he laughs in a thin, embarrassed way, saying he is just tired. Inside, he feels detached, as if his body is still standing in the meeting room but the rest of him is somewhere else, watching from a distance.

The stalking continues for months. He changes routes to work, then changes buses, then starts paying for rides he cannot really afford. He studies reflections in shop windows. He sits in cafés with his back to the wall. Every unknown face begins to feel potentially dangerous. He starts scanning entrances before he can pay attention to anything else. When friends ask him to come out, he makes excuses. It is easier to stay home, though home no longer feels safe either.

His work changes too. UX design had once been the place where he felt most capable-clean systems, predictable logic, small human problems he could solve. Now he struggles to concentrate on basic tasks. He rereads the same user research notes without absorbing them. During design reviews, sudden notification sounds make his shoulders jerk. He keeps his status offline and his camera covered when he is at home. He spends hours checking privacy settings, then checking them again, knowing it does not calm him for long.

What troubles him almost as much as the fear is the shame. He thinks he should have handled it better, should have seen the danger earlier, should not still be this affected. He is young, physically healthy, outwardly functioning. People tell him to ignore it, to log off, to be careful. Their advice makes him feel more alone. He stops telling most people how bad it is. Even with family, he gives edited versions. He does not want them to hear how frightened he is walking home in daylight.

In the present, the stalking has reduced, but his body has not understood that. He still jolts when his phone vibrates. He still checks locks repeatedly before bed and listens for footsteps outside his door. Sleep comes in fragments, interrupted by dreams in which he is being watched and cannot find where the gaze is coming from. Sometimes on the bus he catches sight of someone looking at him and is suddenly back in those months, pulse pounding, palms wet, mind racing ahead to escape routes.

He misses the version of himself who moved through the world without calculation. Now every app, every street, every stranger carries a layer of threat. He wants to focus on typography, wireframes, the pleasure of making something intuitive for other people. Instead, much of his energy goes into trying to feel unobserved, trying to trust an ordinary day, trying to believe that when he closes the door behind him, he is finally alone.
